newsitem.title: UK: POLL-Labour still ahead on economy-Reuters/NOP.
newsitem.headline: POLL-Labour still ahead on economy-Reuters/NOP.

text.p: Britain's opposition Labour party continues to lead the Conservative party on key economic issues ahead of the May 1 election, but the gap between the parties has narrowed, a Reuters poll published on Monday showed.

The survey, conducted by leading poll organisation NOP, found 34 percent of voters trust Labour most to manage the economy, against 29 percent backing the Conservatives. Labour's lead of five points on the question compares with a nine point lead in March and a Conservative lead of two points in February.

NOP polled 1,088 voters across 52 constituencies last Friday. The results suggest the Conservatives are starting to benefit from a growing perception the economy is doing well, but not enough to repair their damaged reputation for economic competence.

Labour's electoral performance was handicapped by economic policy failures when the party was last in power between 1974-79, but now voters appear more mindful of Conservative economic policy problems, particularly sterling's ignominous exit from Europe's exchange rate mechanism in 1992.

But the Conservatives have managed to close Labour's lead significantly on the question of economic management in one of the most influential electoral groups -- the so-called "C2" skilled manual workers, many of whom gave their support to the ruling Conservatives in the past four UK elections.
Labour still enjoys a large 12 point lead in the C2 group in the latest poll, but down sharply from a 32 point lead in the last Reuters/NOP poll conducted in March.

Managerial and professional workers in the AB socio-demographic groups still back the Conservatives on economic management by 44 percent to 24 percent, a lead of 20 points against 21 in the last survey.
The Reuters/NOP poll also asked voters under which party they would be better off, taking into account what they spend, taxes and their income from work, benefits and pensions.
Labour again registered a clear lead of seven points, but narrower than the 14 point lead they enjoyed in the last survey published on March 18.
Labour has been trying to ditch its reputation as a tax-and-spend party and has pledged not to raise the main rates of income tax during the next parliament if it wins the election.

But again the Conservatives are closing the gap on this key issue among skilled manual workers, who make up a large share of Britain's floating, or undecided, voters. The latest survey shows these C2 skilled manual workers backing Labour by 37 to 24 percent on the question, a lead of 13 points against 35 in the last survey.
